newsitem.title: USA: Enron Oil reserves up 10 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Enron Oil reserves up 10 pct in 1996.

text.p: Enron Oil & Gas Co said proved reserves totaled 4.006 trillion cubic feet of natural gas equivalent at year-end 1996, up 10 percent compared to 3.645 trillion at year-end 1995.
The company, 53 percent owned by Enron Corp said exploration and development spending was some $608 million for 1996 and is expected to be about the same in 1997.

"Nearly 40 percent of EOG's 1996 exploration and development expenditures were expended in the fourth quarter, adding significant incremental production capacity in a higher price environment," the company said.

Enron Oil said its total natural gas deliveries averaged 830 million cubic feet per day in 1996, up 12 percent compared to 743 million in 1995. North America wellhead natural gas delivered volumes averaged 706 million cubic feet daily last year, up 11 percent from 636 million in 1995.
Enron Oil said it received average wellhead natural gas prices of $1.78 per thousand cubic feet in 1996 an increase of 38 percent from $1.29 in 1995.
North America wellhead natural gas prices increased 43 percent to $1.92 per thousand cubic feet, the company said.

Enron Oil said its January 1997 U.S. wellhead natural gas prices are expected to average about $4.00 per thousand cubic feet, including wellhead prices in the Big Piney area of Wyoming in the $3.90 range.
Enron Oil said it has consistently utilized a hedging strategy to protect profitability when prices fall, however, it gives up a portion of the increase when prices rise.
In 1996, about 47 percent of the price related increase in wellhead revenues was offset by lower other marketing revenues related to natural gas and crude oil price hedging.

Swap and basis transactions went from a $39.4 million addition in revenue in 1995 to a $44.1 million reduction in revenue in 1996. Other marketing revenues also included reduced margins from other long-term marketing contracts and lower margins associated with the amortization of volumetric production payment deferred revenues.

In line with its hedging strategy, the company said, it entered into natural gas price swaps covering a portion of 1997 production. In December 1996, with the indication of the potential for a significant increase in natural gas prices, a substantial portion of these price swaps for 1997 was closed.

The removal of the hedges will result in revenue reductions of about $56 million in 1997 ($36 million, $9 million, $7 million and $4 million in the first, second, third and fourth quarters of 1997, respectively), which will be offset by any wellhead price increases.
Enron Oil said it now has essentially no natural gas price swaps in place for 1997 after first quarter.
The company said its proven reserves in both 1996 and 1995 include 1.18 trillion cubic feet of proved undeveloped methane reserves contained in deep, Paleozoic era formations in Big Piney, Wyoming.

"We are very pleased to report another great year in replacing production with new reserves on an all sources natural gas equivalent basis achieving a ratio of 201 percent in total, including 137 percent in North America and 500 percent outside North America," the company said.

Most of the reserve adds come from drilling and workover programs which replaced 164 percent of production in total, including 123 percent in North America and 357 percent outside North America. ((-- Jim Brumm 212-859-1710.))
